data.title: Gator Capital Management Q3 2026 Investor Letter
data.description:
Dear Gator Partners:

We are pleased to provide you with the 2026 3rd quarter investor letter for Gator Financial Partners, LLC, Gator Offshore Partners, Ltd., and Gator Qualified Partners, LLC (collectively, the “Funds”). This letter reviews our 2026 Q3 performance, discusses our current view on the French banks, the threat of AI to the cost of bank deposits, the potential end of the Fed Put, and shares our investment thesis on TPG (TPG).

Review of Q3 2026

During the 3rd quarter of 2026, the Funds lagged both the broader market and the Financials sector.

Our long positions in Jackson Financial (JXN), Global Payments (GPN), Navient (NAVI), Ameriprise (AMP), and WEX (WEX) were the top contributors to the Funds’ performance. The largest detractors were long positions in Compass (COMP), Société Générale (SCGLY), Fidelity National Information Services (FIS), Upstart Holdings (UPST), and PROG Holdings (PRG).

Financial stocks performed poorly in the back half of August and September as the 10-year Treasury yield rose more than 60 bps. The companies in our portfolio continue to perform well from a fundamental standpoint. We suffered from multiple compression without any earnings degradation. We see compelling valuations throughout our portfolio.

French Banks: Country Risk Versus Company Fundamentals

Société Générale and BNP Paribas (BNPQY), our two largest positions, were detractors during the third quarter, and their weakness continued into October. France's political unrest, persistent budget deficits, and widening government-bond spreads weighed heavily on both stocks. We believe the decline has created a growing disconnect between their stock prices and their underlying businesses.

Shorting a country's banks is a common way for macro investors to express a negative view on that country. Banks are liquid, economically sensitive, and closely associated with their home markets. We believe French banks have become vehicles for this trade, with investors selling them as proxies for France's political and fiscal problems.

Those problems are real. France is running budget deficits above 5% of GDP, and its fragmented political system has struggled to agree on measures to narrow the gap. The presidential election in April and May 2027 leaves several more months of uncertainty, and an election alone will not necessarily resolve the budget impasse. Nevertheless, Moody's decision in October to maintain France's credit rating offered some reassurance amid the negative headlines.

Our investment cases for the French banks depend primarily on improvements within the banks themselves. Both companies are pursuing greater efficiency, better capital allocation, and higher returns on tangible equity. Their latest results demonstrate continued progress. Société Générale reported a nine-month return on tangible equity of 12.3%, with operating expenses down 3.2%. BNP Paribas reported a nine-month return on tangible equity of 13.2%. These results contrast with the deterioration implied by their share prices.

We believe investors overestimate the banks' direct exposure to French sovereign debt and their dependence on domestic earnings. French government bonds represent less than 1% of total assets at each bank. Both operate diversified international businesses, although Société Générale has greater domestic exposure than BNP Paribas. Small sovereign-bond holdings do not eliminate risks from higher funding costs, taxation, or a weaker French economy, but they materially distinguish these banks from institutions caught in earlier European sovereign-debt crises.

Based on our earnings estimates, both stocks trade at approximately 6.5 times earnings despite generating returns on tangible equity in the low teens. We believe comparable banks operating without the French political discount command approximately nine times earnings. Our longer-term valuation targets remain 1.5 times tangible book value, implying roughly 80% upside from current prices.

Capital returns strengthen the investment case while we wait. Société Générale completed a €1.5 billion extraordinary buyback in September, and BNP Paribas announced a €1.3 billion buyback beginning in November. Repurchasing shares below tangible book value increases tangible book value per remaining share.

We purchased both positions in early 2025 at lower valuations and have earned substantial gains. They became large positions through outperformance. Their recent declines have affected our results, but we remain encouraged by their operational improvements. We believe the depressed valuations support substantial remaining upside. While stabilization in the French bond market is likely necessary for these stocks to stabilize, we don't believe a full retrace in yields or resolution of France's budgetary concerns are needed for these stocks to perform well.

AI, Cash Sorting, and Bank Deposit Franchises

In September, there was a brief research blurb published by Torsten Slok, the Chief Economist at Apollo Global Management (APO), that was picked up by major news outlets saying that banks are at risk of rising deposit costs because customers will use AI agents to optimize the interest they earn on their excess cash. In the unlikely scenario all consumers rapidly optimize their deposit balances, we would have some negative exposure. However, we don't believe this change will take place as rapidly as feared or that every bank is equally exposed to that risk.

We are long banks, but our long exposure is generally concentrated in small- and mid-cap banks that are more focused on commercial customers. The large-cap banks tend to have the strongest consumer deposit franchises, and we are currently net short the large banks. That positioning should make us somewhat less exposed to the specific risk discussed in the article.

We also think the distinction between consumer and commercial deposits is important. AI-driven "cash sorting" is a larger risk to consumer deposits. Businesses already tend to manage their cash much more actively. We have heard several banks say that roughly 80% of their commercial deposits are already indexed or otherwise sensitive to market interest rates. In other words, banks are already paying something close to a market rate on a large portion of their commercial deposits. The bigger potential change would be consumers becoming much more efficient about moving idle balances out of low-yielding checking and savings accounts.

We believe it is important to look at the holistic economics of a banking relationship. Many banks with commercial customers might pay a lower rate than Fed Funds on deposits which appears unoptimized from an outsider's perspective. The truth is many of these deposit customers also have borrowing relationships with the banks. These companies value the capital availability, service and expertise of high-quality banking franchises much more than an incremental 50 bps on deposit balances. Realistically, if deposits were to reprice closer to the Fed Funds rate, then loan spreads would probably move higher as most banks are pricing to a return on each relationship.

The key question, in our view, is how quickly does consumer behavior change. The technology to earn more on idle cash already exists. For example, many brokerage accounts have had interest bearing accounts linked to checking accounts for roughly 20 years or longer. Cash deposited into these brokerage accounts is automatically invested in a money-market fund, while small checking account balances are held at a local bank for ATM access and other banking services. This has been easy to do for a long time, yet most consumers have not chosen to manage their cash this way.

AI agents could certainly reduce the friction and make cash optimization much easier. But there is still an adoption question: How quickly will consumers become comfortable allowing an AI agent to move their money among financial institutions automatically? We would expect the transition will be gradual rather than instantaneous. During earnings calls in October, several banks addressed this concern directly, saying they are blocking AI agents from accessing customer accounts because they are not yet comfortable with the customer verification process. We also believe regulators will need several years to develop comfort with AI agents given the possibility that AI agents moving deposits could trigger bank runs.

More broadly, we view the issue raised in the article as another competitive pressure on the banking industry. We have discussed our view that banks are generally average-to-below-average businesses. They operate in a highly competitive industry, and the competitive intensity continues to increase. Banks like JPMorgan Chase (JPM), PNC Financial (PNC), and Citigroup are entering new cities by hiring teams from other banks and building branches, not by buying smaller banks. This increased bank-on-bank competition increases the competitive intensity. Additionally, non-bank financial companies and fintechs are constantly innovating and trying to capture pieces of the economics that historically accrued to banks. AI-enabled cash management is another example of technology potentially clipping the edges of banks' profitability.

The competitive intensity of the banking industry is one reason we are very valuation-conscious when investing in banks. We do not assume that historically cheap deposit funding will remain permanently cheap. We want to own banks where the valuation, earnings power, customer relationships, and balance sheet compensate us for those competitive risks. We also prefer banks that generate high returns on equity and rely on organic loan and deposit growth.

Testing the Fed Put

Financial stocks weakened in September as Treasury yields rose sharply, with the 10-year yield approaching 5.3% at quarter-end. We believe part of this move reflected investors testing the Federal Reserve's willingness to tolerate market declines under its new Chairman, Kevin Warsh.

Warsh succeeded Jerome Powell in May. In his August Jackson Hole speech, Warsh argued for a different relationship between the Fed and financial markets, with less reliance on forward guidance and more limited use of unconventional monetary policy outside genuine crises. We interpret his comments as an effort to weaken investors' expectation commonly called the "Fed Put": the belief that the central bank will ease policy when asset prices fall sufficiently.

There is an essential distinction between maintaining a functioning financial system and supporting asset prices. The Fed has a responsibility to help ensure that the financial system's plumbing, such as Treasury trading, repo financing, and payments, operates smoothly. Disruptions in these markets can cascade into a broader capital markets shut down and interfere with the transmission of monetary policy. Addressing those disruptions serves a different purpose from intervening because investors dislike the prices at which markets are clearing.

Over time, repeated Fed interventions have encouraged investors to assume that substantial market declines will eventually bring a supportive Fed response. We believe Warsh wants investors to take greater responsibility for pricing and bearing risk. September's bond selloff may have been an early test of that resolve: how far could yields rise before the Fed felt compelled to respond? Inflation uncertainty, Treasury supply, and expectations for short-term interest rates also influenced the move. Nevertheless, uncertainty about the new Chairman's reaction to market stress likely contributed.

Financial stocks struggled with the speed of the adjustment. Although higher yields can benefit certain financial businesses, a sudden increase can pressure valuations, raise funding costs, and renew concerns about securities portfolios and borrowers' ability to refinance. In our assessment, the selloff reflected these concerns more than a deterioration in underlying business performance. Subsequent third-quarter earnings have generally reinforced our view that operating trends remained healthy, without the broad deterioration in credit quality that falling share prices might have suggested.

The backdrop has become more favorable during the fourth quarter. By late October, the 10-year Treasury yield had retreated below 5%, alongside more encouraging inflation readings and demand for Treasuries as technology stocks weakened. For now, the market appears less focused on testing the limits of Fed support.

That does not settle whether the Fed Put has disappeared. It does help to explain why financial stocks finished the third quarter poorly despite generally resilient fundamentals. Our focus remains on distinguishing changes in market expectations from changes in the earnings power and credit quality of the businesses we own.

Investment Thesis on TPG Inc. ("TPG")

In the third quarter we initiated a position in TPG. We see several tailwinds for alternative asset manager earnings over the next few years and believe that TPG is well positioned to benefit. The stock is currently trading at cycle low valuations with a robust opportunity set across their core competencies (private equity, institutional), and emerging growth segments (private credit, wealth, insurance). We believe TPG will benefit disproportionately from the tailwinds present in the industry as well as shifting market perception from a niche private equity specialist to an industry titan with exposures in all fundraising and product segments.

Sector tailwinds

We believe alternative asset managers represent a unique opportunity set over the next several years with discounted valuations, secular growth opportunities, and accelerating realizations.

We see tailwinds from continued growth in the private wealth channel and potential Department of Labor guidance on 401(k) inclusion. The longer duration of 401(k) assets is a natural fit for private equity, even more so than the existing wealth product suite. Because companies are staying private longer, a substantial amount of value creation now occurs outside of the public markets (e.g. OpenAI (OPENAI), Anthropic, Stripe, SpaceX). At the same time, the market's focus on quarterly results has become an obstacle to longer-term investment in certain industries. These factors lead us to believe there is structural alpha in private assets, particularly when those assets are matched with an equally long duration investor base. We view continued wealth channel penetration and broader 401(k) inclusion as a significant opportunity for alternative asset managers, and we believe that opportunity has been obscured by recent concerns around private credit quality and redemptions in semi-liquid wealth vehicles.

We are also encouraged by public market valuations for software companies and other AI exposed industries. Withdrawals from semi-liquid private credit vehicles have continued to slow, and we believe will soon stop weighing on growth and valuations. Ultimately, we think it will benefit the industry to have experienced a redemption cycle as the channel develops. In our view it is healthy for participants to experience the liquidity limitations of private assets firsthand so they can calibrate the liquidity tradeoff for clients as the channel grows.

The M&A environment for sponsors has been relatively quiet for the last several years but with uncertainty emerging about the regulatory environment post 2028, and continued pressure from investors to return and recycle capital we believe the stage is set for an acceleration in both investments and realizations by alternative asset managers. Over the next several years alternative asset firms will monetize significant unrealized performance fees which will be an incremental earnings tailwind alongside continued management fee growth.

Platform Expansion

The market still prices TPG as an institutionally funded, private equity firm. This helps explain why it trades near the average of peers despite its fee related earnings ((“FRE”)) growth being best in class. Investors view an alternative asset manager’s product suite depth as an essential component when evaluating the quality of the business, and private credit has been one of the industry’s fastest growing segments. We do not view TPG as a monoline manager and think we are in the middle innings of this platform expansion. Currently, the company is over indexed to institutional capital (92% of assets), and under indexed to the insurance and wealth channels. TPG is a recent entrant in the credit space after acquiring Angelo Gordon in 2023, but they have doubled credit AUM since the acquisition.

We are optimistic about growth in the wealth channel for the industry and don’t believe this will be a winner takes all market. Given the high level of redemptions out of closed-end private credit funds in the wealth channel that took place early this year, we think advisors will reevaluate the alternative funds they are offering to clients. We think TPG will be a net beneficiary of that reshuffling. In other words, we think TPG provides a competitive alternative to some of the legacy offerings of their competitors.

Prior to the Angelo Gordon acquisition, the company’s AUM was nearly 80% private equity, today that percentage is closer to 50%. In 2025 TPGs credit business grew fee-paying AUM by 23%. Our view is that the monoline perception is outdated and TPG will continue to grow above industry levels in private credit.

Given TPG's smaller base in the wealth channel and private credit, strong industry growth and modest share gains should drive outsized AUM and FRE growth over the next several years.

Flagship fundraising and performance strength

We have been impressed with TPGs track record of flagship fundraising, growing successive funds across their different verticals. Below are a few recent fundraising results we think demonstrate this thesis.

TPG X: $14B raised to date 15% above the predecessor fund

TPG Rise Climate II: Fund raised $8.5B +16% vs predecessor with full program raising $11.4B

Trep V: First close already at $5B vs predecessor at $7B

Credit Solutions III: Raised $6B and was nearly 2x predecessor fund

TPG expects to double credit AUM to $200B by the end of 2029, and they have targeted $55B in total fundraising this year.

As they discussed on their most recent earnings call, TPG's asset flows are becoming less dependent on lumpy flagship fundraising vehicles. We believe a consistent fundraising engine across cycles is a driver of premium multiples for some of their peers.

We view performance as perhaps the most important leading indicator of further demand. TPG funds have performed well versus competitors specifically in their core private equity funds, consistently generating mid-teens IRRs. Strong private credit performance is notable, and this supports our view that they will continue to take market share.

FRE growth and margin opportunity

Analysts expect TPG to grow assets under management in the high teens over the next couple of years. While impressive we view this growth as quite conservative given the tailwinds detailed above.

Coupled with the compelling growth opportunity of the top line, TPG is targeting significant FRE margin expansion over the next few years. TPG is targeting 48% FRE margin for 2026, up from 45% in 2025, and we believe margins of 50% are achievable by 2027. Margins may keep expanding from there as they continue growing assets on a relatively fixed cost base.

We think asset managers generally will realize margin benefits from AI initiatives. Leveraging AI to do deeper diligence on companies at a faster rate should boost margins over time.

Incentive realizations and investment acumen

TPG's earnings are poised to benefit from unrealized carry within its funds. We believe that the next few years could represent a large realization period for all alternative asset managers. TPG specifically has about 7% of market cap sitting in unrealized carry which is equivalent to 1.3x FY25 after tax distributable earnings. TPG realized $205M in carry in FY25, monetizing the current balance over the next three years would roughly double that pace.

Post 2021, there has been a slowdown in private equity monetization activities. With the recent move in yields and geopolitical volatility, there is a concern that this M&A logjam will persist longer. In 2021 TPG’s PE business had realizations reach almost 30% of total AUM vs peers in the high teens to low 20s. In the trough years of 2024–25, TPG still realized 10% of total AUM and 9% of its private equity AUM annually, in line with peers. We like TPG's earnings upside in a robust sponsor M&A market, but we are comfortable with their ability to continue to monetize assets even if tougher conditions persist.

One of the drivers of the selloff in alternative asset managers early this year was the perception that managers had invested heavily in software businesses that would be negatively impacted by AI. TPG was particularly targeted by this narrative as they are known as technology specialists and have 11% of their assets in software. We view software and other AI-affected industries as rapidly changing and we anticipate a wide divergence in outcomes across these industries. We believe TPG’s expertise in software leaves them better positioned than peers to navigate this environment.

Discounted valuation

The alternative asset manager sector represents a compelling buying opportunity with many peers trading at 20%+ discounts to 5-year multiples, with significant forward earnings growth still expected. Most of the group currently trades under a 1x PEG ratio.

TPG specifically is trading at a 20% discount to its average next twelve months of distributable earnings ((“DE”)) multiple which has averaged 18x since its IPO. Shares are down 27% YTD with '27 EPS estimates only down 4%. TPG offers the fastest FRE growth profile among peers and trades around the median multiple.

Risks

Here are the risks we see to our TPG investment thesis:

Stock-based compensation and dilution - TPG excludes equity-based compensation from its reported fee-related earnings (FRE) and distributable earnings (DE). Some of that expense is acquisition-related and should fade, but recurring equity awards are a real cost to shareholders. If the diluted share count continues to rise, strong growth in firmwide earnings may translate into more modest growth in earnings per share. We therefore pay particular attention to per-share earnings growth.

A slower recovery in sponsor M&A - Higher long-term rates make acquisitions harder to finance and can widen the gap between what buyers are willing to pay and what sellers are willing to accept. If exits take longer than we expect, TPG will realize less carried interest in the near term and return less cash to limited partners. That can also slow fundraising for successor funds as investors wait for distributions before making new commitments.

Renewed redemptions in private credit wealth products - Redemption requests have moderated, but weaker credit performance or renewed concerns about liquidity could prompt another wave. Limits on quarterly repurchases can slow outflows, but persistent requests could discourage advisors from directing new money to these products. That would make it harder for TPG to grow its wealth business, even if its own funds perform well.

Slower insurance allocations to private credit - Insurers are an important source of long-duration capital for alternative managers. If tighter capital requirements, less attractive yields relative to public bonds, or greater scrutiny of illiquid assets cause insurers to slow new allocations, industry assets under management could grow more slowly. For TPG, fewer new mandates or slower deployment would delay growth in fee-earning assets and FRE. Jackson Financial's $12 billion minimum commitment provides a base, but growth beyond that commitment and across other insurers remains less certain.

AI disruption in software - TPG disclosed that software accounted for 11% of firmwide AUM, with most of that exposure in private equity. If AI weakens pricing power or customer retention at portfolio companies, earnings and exit multiples could fall together. TPG's software expertise may help it distinguish durable businesses from vulnerable ones, but losses in a few large investments could still reduce carried interest, weaken fund returns, and make the next fundraising cycle harder.

Conclusion

Thank you for entrusting us with a portion of your wealth. We are grateful to you, our investors, who believe in and trust our strategy. On a personal level, Derek Pilecki, the Fund's Portfolio Manager, continues to invest more than 80% of his liquid net worth in the Fund.

As always, we welcome the opportunity to speak with you and discuss the Fund.

Sincerely,

Gator Capital Management, LLC

OVERVIEW

Gator Financial Partners, LLC, Gator Financial Partners Offshore, Ltd., and Gator Qualified Partners, LLC (the “Funds”) are long/short equity hedge funds focused on the Financials sector. The portfolios are built by performing intensive bottom-up fundamental research on both long and short positions. The Funds are concentrated on the portfolio manager’s highest conviction ideas.

The Funds favor small and mid-cap companies and companies with less research coverage from the sell-side. The sector requires specialized knowledge to correctly analyze the companies. Therefore, the portfolio manager believes there are regular opportunities for sector specialists doing fundamental research.

The Fund’s goal is to maximize total return while accepting short-term periods of volatility due to the portfolio’s concentration.
